opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think people conflate two different things. One is whether language models are useful, and they clearly are for some things: autocomplete for code, brainstorming, drafting boilerplate text. I've never denied that. The other is whether the economics and the expectations around them are sustainable, and that's where I think the danger lies.

An AI winter isn't really about the technology vanishing. Expert systems didn't vanish in the late eighties; they were useful in narrow niches and some of them kept running for years. The winter came because the promises vastly outstripped what was delivered, and the money dried up when people realized that. That's the pattern I worry about now.

Right now the valuations and the capital expenditures are predicated on the idea that we're on a short path to artificial general intelligence, that these systems will replace huge swaths of knowledge work, that you can trust them to act autonomously as agents. But the underlying problems haven't gone away. They still hallucinate. They still fail at reliable reasoning, especially outside the distribution of what they've been trained on. They don't have robust world models, so they make errors no human would make, and you can't predict when. For a lot of high-value applications, medicine, law, driving, anything where errors are costly, "mostly right" just isn't good enough.

So you can have a situation where there are real, modest applications, maybe generating some billions of dollars in revenue, but hundreds of billions have gone into data centers and chips. If the revenue doesn't come close to justifying that, investors pull back. And when they pull back, they don't carefully distinguish between the overhyped stuff and the genuinely promising research. Everything gets tarred with the same brush. That's what happened before, and that's what makes it a winter rather than just a correction.

There's another wrinkle too. These models are increasingly commoditized. If lots of companies can build roughly equivalent models, prices fall toward zero, and the margins aren't there to pay back the enormous investments. Useful but cheap doesn't rescue an industry that was priced as if it were going to be transformative and monopolistic.

What I'd like to see, and what would actually protect against a winter, is diversifying our bets: investing in neurosymbolic approaches, in systems that actually represent knowledge and reason over it, rather than putting essentially all of our chips on scaling. Usefulness at the margins won't save us if the core promise turns out to be oversold.

r001.rationale: The response says modest applications could generate billions while hundreds of billions go to infrastructure, leaving investors disappointed if revenue does not justify the investment.

r002.rationale: It explains that investors may pull back and that their reaction can spread beyond overhyped products to promising research.

r003.rationale: Medicine is mentioned as a high-value area where errors matter, but the response does not say socially valuable medical AI could lose funding because its financial returns fail to justify its costs.

r004.rationale: The response leaves open whether useful applications can prevent a winter, saying usefulness at the margins may not save the industry if its core promise is oversold.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think people conflate two different things. One is whether a technology is useful, and the other is whether it lives up to the expectations and the investment that have been poured into it. Those are not the same question. Language models are clearly useful for some things. I use them myself for brainstorming, for drafting, for coding assistance, where a human is checking the output. Nobody serious is saying they're useless. But "useful" and "worth the hundreds of billions of dollars that have been bet on them" are very different claims.

If you look at the history of AI winters, they didn't happen because the technology did nothing. Expert systems in the eighties actually worked for narrow problems. Companies deployed them. The winter came because the promises were much bigger than what was delivered, and when the gap became undeniable, the money dried up. That's the dynamic I worry about. The pitch right now isn't "here's a nice autocomplete for programmers." The pitch is AGI, agents that run your business, replacing knowledge workers, trillions in value. And the core problems haven't gone away. These systems still hallucinate. They still can't reliably reason. They still fail on distribution shift in ways that are hard to predict, and you can't deploy something that's right ninety percent of the time in a context where the ten percent is catastrophic.

So you can have a world where the technology is genuinely helpful in a lot of modest ways, and still have a financial collapse, because the valuations were built on something else entirely. The useful applications don't pay for the data centers. And when the investors realize that, the funding contracts, the research gets starved, and we get a winter anyway, even though the tools are still sitting there being moderately helpful. In some ways that's the most likely scenario: not that LLMs vanish, but that they settle into being one component among many, and the hype cycle crashes around them. And I'd add that a winter would be a shame, because we need the resources to go into the approaches, neurosymbolic ones, for example, that could actually address the reliability problems. A crash doesn't discriminate between the overhyped and the promising.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes useful applications such as drafting and coding assistance from being worth the hundreds of billions investors have committed, and says expectations may exceed what is delivered.

r002.rationale: It says investors may pull funding when they realize useful applications do not justify the valuations, potentially triggering a winter.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention medical AI or socially valuable medical applications losing funding because their returns fail to cover costs.

r004.rationale: It presents a winter despite useful applications as a likely possibility, rather than asserting that practical applications will certainly prevent one.

astra-6.text:
Well, useful applications and an AI winter aren't mutually exclusive. An AI winter doesn't mean that nothing works. It means that expectations and investment have gotten ahead of what the technology can deliver, and then there's a retrenchment.

You can have language models that are useful for drafting things, helping with programming, and so forth, without having systems that are reliable enough to do all the jobs people imagine they'll do. If you have to check everything that comes out, that affects the economics. A compelling demonstration isn't necessarily a viable business.

So the question isn't just, “Does this technology have any value?” Of course it does. The question is whether that value justifies the enormous expectations and expenditures. If people are investing on the assumption that we're about to get artificial general intelligence, and what they actually get is a useful but unreliable assistant, there can still be a very substantial correction. The useful applications can survive that correction.

r001.rationale: The response says useful but unreliable language model applications may fall short of AGI-scale expectations, leading to an investment correction despite their practical value.

r002.rationale: It explicitly connects investor assumptions about AGI and the scale of investment to whether useful applications avert a substantial correction.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss medical AI, social value, or funding decisions based on medical AI’s costs and financial returns.

r004.rationale: The response says useful applications can coexist with an AI winter and describes a correction as possible, leaving open whether practical applications will be enough to prevent one.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, useful technology and a sustainable business are two different things. You can have real applications and still have an enormous gap between what the technology delivers and what investors have been led to expect. If you spend vast sums building these systems, but customers won’t pay enough to cover those costs, having some useful applications doesn’t solve the economic problem.

And there’s a technical issue, too. A system can be useful for brainstorming or writing a first draft without being reliable enough to run a business process autonomously. If somebody has to check everything it does, that limits the value. The leap from producing plausible language to consistently getting things right is substantial.

So an AI winter doesn’t require that the technology be useless. It requires expectations to outrun results, followed by a loss of confidence and funding. Some applications could survive and flourish while the broader investment boom collapses.

r001.rationale: The response says useful applications can coexist with a gap between delivered value and investor expectations, and that customers may not pay enough to cover the costs.

r002.rationale: It connects expectations, loss of confidence, and funding to whether useful applications prevent a broader AI winter.

r003.rationale: The response discusses costs and returns generally but does not mention medical AI or its social value.

r004.rationale: It says useful applications could survive while the broader investment boom collapses, leaving practical applications’ ability to forestall a winter uncertain.
